flashcards.front: Why should GeoDNS records for regional failover use a low TTL (e.g., 30–60s) instead of 24 hours?
flashcards.back: Recursive ISP and client resolvers cache DNS records for the full TTL. A 24-hour TTL leaves users routed to a dead region long after health checks fail; a 60s TTL limits failover lag while balancing resolver query load.

flashcards.front: What problem does an Origin Shield solve in a global Pull CDN?
flashcards.back: When a popular uncached object is requested across 50 edge PoPs simultaneously, an Origin Shield acts as a regional L2 collapsing cache so only 1 request hits your origin instead of 50.

flashcards.front: Why do multiplexed HTTP/2 and gRPC connections require an L7 load balancer between pods?
flashcards.back: An L4 balancer routes per TCP connection (5-tuple). Because HTTP/2 and gRPC multiplex hundreds of RPCs over one long-lived TCP connection, L4 pins all traffic to one backend pod; L7 inspects and balances individual streams/requests.

flashcards.front: How does PEWMA (Peak Exponentially Weighted Moving Average) improve over Round Robin?
flashcards.back: PEWMA combines active in-flight requests with exponentially smoothed backend response times, automatically shifting traffic away from slow or GC-paused 'gray failure' pods.

flashcards.front: Why execute Token Bucket check-and-decrement inside a Redis Lua script?
flashcards.back: Separate GET then SET calls across concurrent gateway pods cause race conditions (double-spending tokens). Redis executes Lua scripts atomically on its single-threaded event loop without distributed lock overhead.

flashcards.front: When should a distributed rate limiter fail-open vs fail-closed if Redis goes unreachable?
flashcards.back: Fail-open (with an in-memory per-pod soft cap) for revenue/consumer APIs so a Redis blip never causes a total outage; fail-closed for strict security, anti-fraud, or compliance quotas.

flashcards.front: Distinguish Cache Penetration, Cache Stampede (Thundering Herd), and Cache Avalanche.
flashcards.back: Penetration: queries for non-existent keys miss cache and hit DB (fix: Bloom filter or null-caching). Stampede: 1 hot key expires under heavy concurrency (fix: Singleflight coalescing / soft TTL). Avalanche: many keys expire at once or Redis crashes (fix: jittered TTLs + cluster HA).

flashcards.front: What is the main risk of Write-Behind (Write-Back) caching compared to Write-Through?
flashcards.back: Write-Behind acks writes after updating Redis and flushes asynchronously to the database in batches, risking permanent data loss if the cache node crashes before flushing.

flashcards.front: How many keys move on average when adding 1 node to a N-node Consistent Hashing ring?
flashcards.back: Only ~K/N keys move (only keys falling in the new node's clockwise arcs), compared to ~(N-1)/N keys under naive modulo hashing `hash(key) % N`.

flashcards.front: Why do production hash rings assign 150–200 virtual nodes (vnodes) per physical server?
flashcards.back: With few physical nodes, random hash positions cause severe imbalance; interleaving hundreds of vnodes reduces variance to ~5% and spreads orphaned load evenly across all surviving servers when one node fails.

flashcards.front: How does Raft prevent split-brain when an old Leader gets partitioned and reconnects?
flashcards.back: A majority cluster elects a new Leader at a higher monotonic Term (`T+1`). Any RPC or client heartbeat carrying stale Term `T` is immediately rejected by nodes at `T+1`, forcing the deposed leader to step down.

flashcards.front: What does `W + R > N` guarantee in Dynamo-style quorum replication, and what does it NOT prevent?
flashcards.back: It guarantees every read quorum overlaps at least one node from the latest write quorum. However, concurrent writes or sloppy quorums can still diverge, requiring vector clocks / CRDTs or Last-Write-Wins reconciliation.

flashcards.front: What is the scope of strict message ordering in Apache Kafka?
flashcards.back: Ordering is guaranteed strictly within a single partition—not across an entire multi-partition topic. Partition by entity key (e.g., `order_id`) when ordering per entity matters.

flashcards.front: Why does Kafka scale consumer throughput only up to `N consumers = N partitions` per group?
flashcards.back: To preserve per-partition sequential ordering, each partition is assigned to at most one consumer instance inside a given consumer group. Extra idle consumers sit unused until partition count grows.

flashcards.front: Why must user ACL permissions be enforced BEFORE or INSIDE vector retrieval rather than post-filtering?
flashcards.back: Post-filtering top-K retrieved chunks risks returning zero allowed results when top matches are confidential—and caching or passing unauthorized text into LLM prompts creates severe data-leak vulnerabilities.

flashcards.front: Why pair dense HNSW vector search with sparse BM25 keyword search (Hybrid Retrieval)?
flashcards.back: Dense embeddings capture semantic meaning but often miss exact error codes, SKUs, or acronyms; BM25 nails exact lexical matches. Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) + reranking combines both strengths.

flashcards.front: In a URL shortener, when should you return HTTP 301 vs HTTP 302?
flashcards.back: HTTP 301 (Moved Permanently) makes browsers cache the target directly—saving server QPS but blinding click analytics and preventing link updates. HTTP 302 (Found) hits your server every click for accurate telemetry.

flashcards.front: Why is Hybrid Fan-Out preferred over pure Fan-Out-on-Write for Twitter/X?
flashcards.back: Pushing a single tweet from a 50M-follower celebrity into 50M Redis timelines causes minutes-long queue lag and massive write amplification. Hybrid pushes normal users and merges celebrity posts on read.

flashcards.front: Why do chat servers pair Cassandra with `(chat_id, bucket)` partition keys and Snowflake/seq clustering keys?
flashcards.back: LSM-tree storage handles massive write rates (hundreds of thousands of messages/sec), while partitioning by `(chat_id, month)` keeps single-conversation scroll queries sequential on one shard without unbounded partition growth.

flashcards.front: Why store active moving driver coordinates in city-sharded in-memory H3/Redis rather than Postgres?
flashcards.back: 2M drivers pinging every 4s generate 500k updates/sec, which would overwhelm SQL B-Tree index writes. Yet 2M active records × 64B is only ~128 MB—fitting cleanly in sharded RAM with short TTL expiration.

flashcards.front: How do PagedAttention and Continuous Batching dramatically increase LLM serving throughput?
flashcards.back: Continuous batching schedules requests at each token step instead of waiting for the longest batch sequence to finish, while PagedAttention eliminates >60% KV-cache VRAM fragmentation using non-contiguous memory blocks.

flashcards.front: Why do LSM-Trees convert random writes into fast sequential disk I/O compared to B-Trees?
flashcards.back: Mutations append sequentially to a WAL and insert into an in-memory sorted MemTable, which later flushes sequentially as immutable SSTables—avoiding B-Tree random 4–16 KB page read-modify-writes and page splits.

flashcards.front: How do LSM-Trees avoid probing every SSTable on disk when looking up a non-existent key?
flashcards.back: Each SSTable pairs with a compact in-memory Bloom filter; if the Bloom filter reports negative, that SSTable definitely does not hold the key and is skipped immediately.

flashcards.front: What is Write Skew under Snapshot Isolation (Repeatable Read), and why do normal row locks miss it?
flashcards.back: Two transactions read the same overlapping premise on Snapshot Isolation and update *disjoint* rows (e.g., Alice disables Alice, Bob disables Bob), breaking a cross-row invariant without triggering same-row write conflicts.

flashcards.front: How does Serializable Snapshot Isolation (SSI) stop Write Skew without blocking concurrent readers?
flashcards.back: SSI tracks optimistic `SIREAD` predicate read locks across snapshots and aborts one transaction (SQLSTATE 40001) whenever two concurrent transactions create a mutual read-write antidependency cycle.

flashcards.front: When should you choose Server-Sent Events (SSE) over WebSockets?
flashcards.back: Choose SSE when updates flow one-way from server to browser (notifications, stock tickers, LLM token streams). SSE runs over standard HTTP/2, automatically reconnects with `Last-Event-ID`, and passes corporate proxies cleanly without Upgrade headers.

flashcards.front: How do you broadcast chat or telemetry events across thousands of stateful WebSocket servers?
flashcards.back: Keep each gateway stateless with respect to global room state: attach clients via consistent routing and bridge gateways through a pub/sub backplane (Redis Pub/Sub or Kafka) plus backpressure watermarks to drop or sample slow consumers.

flashcards.front: How does key salting cure a celebrity hot-key partition without breaking reads?
flashcards.back: Append a bounded random suffix (`celebrity_id#0..N-1`) to spread writes across N shards. Reads either fan out across all N salted keys and merge or route through a short-TTL read cache.

flashcards.front: What is the key trade-off between hash partitioning and key-range partitioning?
flashcards.back: Hash partitioning distributes writes evenly and avoids hot spots caused by monotonic timestamps, whereas range partitioning keeps adjacent keys sorted for fast range scans at the risk of hot tail partitions.

flashcards.front: Why is a plain Redis TTL lock (`SET NX PX`) unsafe without a fencing token?
flashcards.back: A client experiencing a stop-the-world GC pause or network delay after acquiring the lock can resume after its TTL expires and overwrite storage while a second client holds the newer lease. Only a monotonically increasing fencing token checked by storage rejects the stale write.

flashcards.front: Who must validate a fencing token to guarantee mutual exclusion under process pauses?
flashcards.back: The downstream storage or resource server itself (for example via `WHERE epoch < :token` or Raft log version checks)—never the lock service alone, because delayed RPCs are already in flight.

flashcards.front: What split-brain hazard does the Transactional Outbox pattern eliminate?
flashcards.back: It eliminates dual-write inconsistency between an OLTP database commit and a Kafka/message-broker publish: both the domain row and an `outbox` event row commit atomically in one local ACID transaction.

flashcards.front: Why prefer log-based CDC (Debezium reading the WAL/binlog) over periodic `SELECT * FROM outbox` polling?
flashcards.back: Log-based CDC tails the append-only database WAL asynchronously with sub-second lag, zero extra read queries on hot OLTP indexes, and preserves exact commit order before consumers deduplicate by `event_id`.

flashcards.front: Why do microservices avoid Two-Phase Commit (2PC) across service boundaries and use Sagas instead?
flashcards.back: 2PC holds locks across all participants during coordinator pauses (`in-doubt` state if the coordinator crashes), coupling availability to every node. A Saga breaks the workflow into local ACID steps paired with idempotent compensating transactions.

flashcards.front: When choosing between Choreography and Orchestration for a multi-step Saga, what is the pragmatic rule?
flashcards.back: Choreography suits simple 2–3 step flows with loose coupling; Orchestration wins beyond ~4 steps or branching failure recovery because one explicit state machine owns timeouts, retries, and compensation order.

flashcards.front: How does an HTTP `Idempotency-Key` ledger safely handle concurrent retries?
flashcards.back: Store `UNIQUE(merchant_id, idempotency_key)` alongside a request payload hash and serialized response: an `IN_PROGRESS` row returns `409 Conflict`, payload mismatches return `422`, and a `COMPLETED` row replays the saved response without re-executing side effects.

flashcards.front: Why must exponential backoff retries always add full jitter and pair with a Circuit Breaker?
flashcards.back: Unjittered retries synchronize into a thundering herd that locks a recovering service at 100% load. Adding jitter spreads retry waves, while an open Circuit Breaker fails fast in <1ms so worker thread pools don't exhaust.

flashcards.front: How do ticketing systems protect the primary SQL database when 500,000 fans click Buy at 10:00:00 AM?
flashcards.back: Put a distributed Virtual Waiting Room token gate in front of checkout so only bounded capacity reaches checkout, and enforce seat uniqueness with a Redis hold TTL plus an ACID unique constraint (`(event_id, seat_id)`) in PostgreSQL.

flashcards.front: What happens if a user's 10-minute seat hold expires in Redis right as their payment webhook settles?
flashcards.back: Re-verify seat status inside a conditional SQL `UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'HELD' AND hold_token = :tok` before finalizing the ticket; if already released or sold to another buyer, trigger an automatic refund rather than double-booking the seat.

flashcards.front: Why do financial ledgers use append-only double-entry journal rows instead of `UPDATE balance = balance - amount`?
flashcards.back: Every transfer records balanced debit and credit entries in an immutable log, guaranteeing `SUM(debits) == SUM(credits)` for cryptographic/accounting audits and safe replay without losing historical provenance.

flashcards.front: How does a payment gateway handle ambiguous timeouts from an external PSP/card network?
flashcards.back: Never assume a timeout means failure: transition the payment intent to `PENDING_RECONCILIATION`, stop blind duplicate charges, pass the same `idempotency_key`, and resolve state via signed webhooks + scheduled T+N settlement file reconciliation.

flashcards.front: Why does adaptive bitrate (ABR) video transcode uploads into multi-bitrate 2–6 second `.m4s` GOP-aligned segments?
flashcards.back: Splitting into independent IDR-aligned segments lets players seamlessly switch between 360p, 1080p, and 4K mid-stream as bandwidth fluctuates, while making each immutable chunk 100% cacheable at CDN edge PoPs and pre-encoded in parallel via a DAG.

flashcards.front: What dual storage strategy keeps CDN hit ratios above 95% for massive VOD catalogs like Netflix?
flashcards.back: Serve the hot 5% zipfian head (new releases/trending shows) from NVMe/SSD Open Connect edge appliances directly inside ISPs, while storing the vast long tail in regional S3/origin shields fetched on miss.

flashcards.front: Why must you NEVER reuse a retired Protobuf or Thrift field tag number?
flashcards.back: Historic persisted messages or older binaries in rolling deployments still map that integer tag to the old field type/semantics, causing silent data corruption when parsed by code expecting the new meaning.

flashcards.front: How does Apache Avro differ from Protocol Buffers on the wire?
flashcards.back: Protobuf embeds numeric field tags on every serialized message; Avro strips even tags from the record body and pairs each binary payload with a 5-byte Schema Registry ID so readers reconcile writer vs reader schemas dynamically.

flashcards.front: If 1 page request fans out in parallel to K=20 backend shards with p99 = 40ms each, what % of page loads hit >40ms tail latency?
flashcards.back: `1 - (0.99)^20 = ~18.2%`! Parallel scatter-gather fan-out amplifies tail-latency impact linearly with fan-out factor unless mitigated by hedged requests and shard deadlines.

flashcards.front: How does Shuffle Sharding improve multi-tenant blast radius isolation over standard partitioning?
flashcards.back: Mapping each tenant to a random subset of K=2 cells out of M=16 pools yields 120 virtual combinations (`M choose K`), ensuring a single toxic tenant saturates <8% of overlap with healthy customers.

flashcards.front: What does an SSTable Bloom Filter optimize in an LSM-Tree engine, and roughly how much RAM does it need?
flashcards.back: A per-SSTable Bloom Filter rejects lookups for non-existent keys in O(1) RAM before touching NVMe disk (~9.6 bits/key for 1% false-positive rate ≈ ~1.2 MB per 1M keys).

flashcards.front: Why do analytics/audit queries achieve >90% I/O savings on Parquet/ClickHouse compared to Postgres rows?
flashcards.back: Columnar formats pack values of each column contiguously using Dictionary Encoding, RLE, and Bitmaps, so a 3-of-40-column scan reads only those 3 compressed stripes via SIMD execution.

flashcards.front: How do Stripe-style date-pinned API versions avoid polluting core billing domain logic with legacy `if/else` checks?
flashcards.back: Push version transformations (`2024-05-01` -> `vCurrent`) cleanly into declarative Edge Contract Adapters (TPP Design by Contract), keeping core services working on a single canonical Protobuf model.

flashcards.front: Why should an HTTP `Idempotency-Key` ledger store a SHA-256 hash of the request payload?
flashcards.back: Detecting payload mismatches lets the API reject accidental key reuse for different billing amounts with `422 Unprocessable Entity` instead of silently replaying the earlier charge receipt.

flashcards.front: What three mathematical properties must CRDT merge functions satisfy to converge identically without locks?
flashcards.back: Associativity, Commutativity, and Idempotence—ensuring any peer network can deliver, reorder, or duplicate deltas across offline partitions and still reach identical final state.

flashcards.front: Contrast Local (Document-Partitioned) vs Global (Term-Partitioned) secondary indexes.
flashcards.back: Local indexes give fast single-shard atomic writes but require scatter-gather reads across ALL shards (p99 hit); Global indexes give O(1) fast shard reads at the cost of async cross-shard write updates.

flashcards.front: Why must stream velocity windows use Event-Time Watermarks rather than Processing-Time clocks?
flashcards.back: Delayed mobile retries arrive minutes late; Event-Time Watermarks (`MaxEventTime - MaxOutOfOrderDelay`) paired with `allowedLateness` evaluate bursts by when transactions actually occurred.

flashcards.front: How do Actor + Blackboard patterns break temporal and structural coupling in streaming systems?
flashcards.back: Keyed Actors maintain lock-free isolated entity state from partitioned streams, publishing independent anomaly signals onto a shared Blackboard coordinator so ML/rule evaluators evolve independently.

quizzes.scenario: Your primary US-East region goes down. Your Route53 health check flips DNS to US-West within 10 seconds, yet 40% of users still hit US-East for 3 hours.
quizzes.question: What is the most likely architectural misconfiguration?
options: Your CDN uses HTTP/3 instead of HTTP/2
Your authoritative DNS record TTL was set too high (e.g., 14400s / 4 hours)
Your Origin S3 bucket lacked cross-region versioning
Your load balancer used Least Connections instead of Round Robin
quizzes.explanation: Recursive DNS resolvers and client OS caches hold the old IP until TTL expires. Keeping failover DNS TTLs low (e.g. 30–60s) bounds stale DNS routing windows.

quizzes.scenario: Every time a breaking news video drops, 80 global CDN edge PoPs simultaneously miss cache and hammer your origin server with 80 identical 50 MB fetches.
quizzes.question: Which CDN pattern directly collapses those 80 edge misses into 1 origin fetch?
options: Switching from HTTPS to HTTP
Disabling Cache-Control max-age headers
Enabling an Origin Shield with request collapsing
Increasing DNS TTL to 24 hours
quizzes.explanation: An Origin Shield sits as a regional L2 tier between edge PoPs and the origin, coalescing concurrent misses for the same cache key into a single origin request.

quizzes.scenario: You scale a gRPC microservice from 4 pods to 12 pods behind a Network Load Balancer (L4), but CPU stays pegged at 95% on the original 4 pods while the 8 new pods sit at 0%.
quizzes.question: Why did traffic fail to distribute to the 8 new pods?
options: L4 load balances per TCP connection, and persistent HTTP/2 gRPC connections stay pinned to the original 4 pods
gRPC only runs over UDP
DNS Round Robin caches pod IPs inside CPU L1 cache
L4 balancers drop TLS 1.3 packets
quizzes.explanation: Because HTTP/2/gRPC multiplexes requests over long-lived TCP connections, an L4 balancer has nothing new to balance unless clients reconnect or an L7 proxy (like Envoy) balances per-RPC stream.

quizzes.scenario: One backend pod enters a 'gray failure': its `/health` endpoint returns HTTP 200 OK, yet real `/checkout` queries take 1,200ms due to garbage collection pauses.
quizzes.question: Which load-balancing mechanism mitigates this fastest without killing healthy traffic?
options: Static Round Robin with 30s active HTTP /health probes
IP Hash sticky sessions
PEWMA (latency-weighted Least Connections) combined with passive outlier detection
Increasing the database connection pool size
quizzes.explanation: PEWMA scores pods by in-flight concurrency × smoothed latency so traffic naturally shifts away from slow pods immediately, while passive outlier detection ejects consecutive errors.

quizzes.scenario: You enforce '100 requests per minute' using a Fixed Window Counter at `:00` minute boundaries. A client sends 100 requests at `12:00:59` and 100 more at `12:01:01`.
quizzes.question: Which rate-limiter flaw allowed 200 requests in 2 seconds, and which algorithm fixes it cleanly with minimal RAM?
options: Fixed Window boundary burst; Sliding Window Counter fixes it using two adjacent buckets
Token Bucket underflow; Leaky Bucket fixes it via DNS
Redis Lua race condition; Mutex locking fixes it
Clock drift; NTP sync fixes it
quizzes.explanation: Fixed windows allow 2x bursts straddling minute boundaries. Sliding Window Counter weights the overlap of the previous and current counters using O(1) memory per key.

quizzes.scenario: Your distributed rate limiter uses Redis. During a 10-second Redis cluster failover, your API Gateway begins returning HTTP 500 to 100% of paying checkout users.
quizzes.question: What policy should a payment/checkout API Gateway implement for rate-limiter dependency faults?
options: Fail-closed to protect Redis memory
Fail-open with a conservative local in-memory per-pod soft limit
Retry Redis 10 times synchronously per request
Redirect users to S3
quizzes.explanation: Rate limiters shouldn't become a single point of total outage for core business revenue; failing open to a per-pod local safety cap keeps checkouts alive.

quizzes.scenario: Attacker bots query millions of random non-existent `product_id`s (`/products/999999123`). Redis misses every time, pushing 100% of attack QPS straight into Postgres.
quizzes.question: Which defense stops this Cache Penetration attack with minimal memory?
options: Increasing Redis LRU eviction aggressiveness
Placing a Bloom Filter (plus short-TTL negative null caching) before DB lookups
Switching from Postgres to Cassandra
Disabling HTTP Keep-Alive
quizzes.explanation: A Bloom filter guarantees zero false negatives for valid IDs—so any ID returning 'not in set' short-circuits immediately with 404 without touching Postgres.

quizzes.scenario: At midnight, 500,000 cached homepage items populated together at noon all hit their exact 12-hour TTL simultaneously, collapsing the database.
quizzes.question: What caused this outage and what prevents it?
options: Cache Avalanche; add random TTL jitter (e.g., 12h + rand(0..30m)) so expirations spread smoothly
Cache Penetration; switch to Write-Through
Split-brain; add Raft
TCP slow start; enable QUIC
quizzes.explanation: Synchronized bulk expiration creates a Cache Avalanche. Adding random jitter to TTLs spreads backfill DB queries evenly.

quizzes.scenario: You scale a 10-node Memcached fleet to 11 nodes using `server = hash(key) % 11` instead of consistent hashing.
quizzes.question: Approximately what fraction of cached keys miss immediately on the next request?
quizzes.explanation: Changing the modulo divisor from 10 to 11 alters `hash(key) % N` for ~10/11 (~91%) of all keys, triggering a massive cache miss avalanche.

quizzes.scenario: Your Consistent Hash ring uses 200 virtual nodes per shard, yet Shard 4 still hits 100% CPU because one celebrity user's profile accounts for 35% of all reads.
quizzes.question: Does adding more virtual nodes fix a single hot key?
options: Yes, more vnodes automatically split a single key across multiple servers
No—a single key still hashes to one ring position; fix with key salting (`key#0..N`) or local L1 caching
Yes, if you switch from SHA-1 to MD5
No, only switching to B-Tree storage fixes it
quizzes.explanation: Vnodes balance key COUNT across shards, not QPS skew on a single key. Hot keys require local pod L1 caching, read replication, or salted key suffix sharding.

quizzes.scenario: A 5-node Raft cluster experiences a network partition splitting `{Node1 (old Leader), Node2}` from `{Node3, Node4, Node5}`.
quizzes.question: Which side can elect a leader and commit new writes while maintaining CP safety?
options: Both sides commit writes independently
Only `{Node1, Node2}` because it holds the original leader
Only `{Node3, Node4, Node5}` because 3 nodes form the majority quorum (floor(5/2) + 1 = 3)
Neither side can process writes
quizzes.explanation: Raft requires a strict majority (3 of 5). The minority partition cannot commit entries, guaranteeing zero split-brain divergence.

quizzes.scenario: In a 3-replica Dynamo-style store (`N=3`), you configure `W=2` and `R=1` to optimize read latency.
quizzes.question: What consistency behavior does `W=2, R=1` give you?
options: Strong linearizable consistency because W > 1
Eventual consistency—a read of R=1 can hit the 1 replica that missed the W=2 write (`2+1 <= 3`)
Zero availability during any single node outage
Guaranteed multi-row ACID transactions
quizzes.explanation: Since `W + R = 3` is NOT strictly greater than `N = 3`, the single read node could be the lagging 3rd replica.

quizzes.scenario: Your `orders` Kafka topic has 8 partitions. You deploy 16 instances in the `billing-group` consumer group to double processing speed, but throughput doesn't budge.
quizzes.question: Why did scaling from 8 to 16 consumer workers give zero speedup?
options: Kafka allows at most 1 consumer per partition within the same consumer group—8 workers are sitting idle
Kafka consumers run single-threaded across the whole cluster
Partition 0 locks all 8 partitions during commits
acks=all blocks consumer polling
quizzes.explanation: In a consumer group, each partition maps to at most one worker to maintain partition ordering. To scale to 16 workers, increase partitions or parallelize downstream work.

quizzes.scenario: An invalid malformed message at offset 500 causes your consumer worker to throw an exception before committing offsets, restarting infinitely every 2 seconds.
quizzes.question: How should production streaming architectures handle this poison-pill message?
options: Auto-commit offsets before processing begins (at-most-once)
Use bounded retries, then publish the bad record with error metadata to a Dead-Letter Topic (DLQ) and advance the offset
Increase acks=all on the producer
Delete the Kafka topic
quizzes.explanation: Quarantining unprocessable records to a monitored DLQ unblocks healthy messages on that partition while preserving failed events for debugging/replay.

quizzes.scenario: In an enterprise RAG assistant, your team fetches the top-10 vector matches globally, sends them to the LLM, and filters out unauthorized citations from the final text.
quizzes.question: Why is this architecture critically flawed?
options: HNSW cannot index PDFs
Confidential text can leak indirectly into the generated answer (or prompt injection) and relevant permitted chunks get crowded out before retrieval
Cross-encoders only work with SQL
SSE doesn't support citations
quizzes.explanation: ACLs must be enforced as pre-filters INSIDE the retriever (and semantic cache key) so unauthorized chunks never enter the LLM context window.

quizzes.scenario: During peak enterprise usage, your frontier 70B GPU cluster saturates KV-cache memory, driving TTFT from 300ms to 6 seconds.
quizzes.question: Which combination best maintains interactive UX and system availability?
options: Remove TPM rate limits and increase request timeout to 60s
Serve high-confidence ACL-scoped Semantic Cache hits and downshift routine queries to a fast quantized SLM fallback
Disable continuous batching
Run cross-encoder reranking on all 10 million documents per query
quizzes.explanation: Semantic caching avoids GPU invocation entirely on common queries, while SLM model routing sheds compute pressure cleanly under saturation.

quizzes.scenario: Marketing asks for per-link country and referrer analytics on every short URL click, alongside instant redirects.
quizzes.question: Which HTTP redirect status and analytics ingestion pattern should you choose?
options: HTTP 301 + synchronous SQL `UPDATE clicks = clicks + 1`
HTTP 302 + async ClickEvent emission to Kafka
HTTP 200 + HTML meta refresh
HTTP 301 + client-side localStorage
quizzes.explanation: 302 routes repeat clicks through your gateway for analytics (unlike browser-cached 301), while Kafka keeps click aggregation off the critical redirect latency path.

quizzes.scenario: Your social app uses pure Fan-Out-on-Write. When an account with 45 million followers posts, normal users wait 12 minutes to see their friends' new posts.
quizzes.question: What caused the delay and how do you fix it?
options: 45M Redis timeline pushes flooded the async fan-out queue; adopt Hybrid Fan-Out (skip push for celebrities and merge on read)
Snowflake IDs ran out of bits; switch to UUIDv4
Postgres SQL OFFSET pagination slowed writes; switch to LIMIT
S3 CDN expired TLS certificates
quizzes.explanation: Hybrid Fan-Out routes celebrities (>10k followers) onto read-time merge from a small replicated/L1-cached celebrity post list, eliminating multi-million-row fan-out spikes.

quizzes.scenario: A Chat Gateway pod holding 100,000 persistent WebSockets crashes. Instantly, 100,000 mobile clients attempt immediate reconnects, crashing your Auth and Session Redis tier.
quizzes.question: What client/edge mitigation stops this reconnect thundering herd?
options: Switch WebSockets to HTTP 301 redirects
Client exponential backoff with randomized full jitter + edge connection rate-shaping
Store messages in local browser cookies only
Use a single global Raft leader for all WebSockets
quizzes.explanation: Adding randomized exponential jitter spreads 100k TLS handshakes smoothly over 10–30 seconds instead of slamming auth/session stores in a 100ms spike.

quizzes.scenario: Two riders tap 'Request Ride' in the same millisecond near the only available driver `d_901`. Both see 'Driver assigned!' and then one gets an error.
quizzes.question: What prevents concurrent double-dispatch without locking an entire city table?
options: Eventual consistency on driver GPS pings
Per-driver atomic Redis lock (`SET lock:driver:d_901 tripId NX EX 15`) before sending the ride offer
Moving driver coordinates into S3
Querying only 1 H3 cell without neighbors
quizzes.explanation: An atomic NX lock with a short offer TTL serializes offers per individual driver in <1ms so only one rider's dispatch flow can offer to `d_901` at a time.

quizzes.scenario: Your API gateway rate-limits users purely at 60 Requests Per Minute (RPM). One heavy user sends 60 concurrent 100k-token document prompts per minute and saturates your entire GPU fleet.
quizzes.question: Which rate-limiting upgrade closes this loophole?
options: Limit by IPv4 subnet only
Enforce dual RPM + TPM (Tokens Per Minute) buckets—reserving estimated tokens upfront and refunding unused output tokens when the SSE stream ends
Switch SSE to HTTP 1.0
Store raw KV tensors in Postgres
quizzes.explanation: GPU compute and KV-cache memory scale with token counts, not just HTTP request counts. Dual RPM + TPM accounting prevents single long-context callers from monopolizing GPUs.

quizzes.scenario: Your Cassandra / RocksDB-backed chat service handles 250k writes/sec smoothly, yet every few minutes point-read p99 spikes from 2ms to 55ms.
quizzes.question: Which DDIA Chapter 3 storage-engine phenomenon most likely explains these periodic p99 spikes?
options: B-Tree page splitting during read operations
Background SSTable compaction competing for NVMe disk bandwidth while overlapping L0 files accumulate
HTTP 301 browser caching
DNS TTL expiration
quizzes.explanation: LSM background compaction rewrites and merges large SSTable segments sequentially, temporarily contending with foreground read IOPS unless compaction bandwidth is throttled.

quizzes.scenario: You deploy a write-heavy LSM KV store using random UUIDv4 keys and observe heavy read latency whenever callers query keys that do not exist yet.
quizzes.question: Which per-SSTable structure cuts wasted disk seeks on non-existent keys?
options: Increasing WAL fsync interval to 10 minutes
In-memory per-SSTable Bloom filters
Removing MemTables completely
Switching to SQL OFFSET pagination
quizzes.explanation: Bloom filters sit in RAM per SSTable and deterministically identify when a key is definitely absent from that disk segment.

quizzes.scenario: Under PostgreSQL `REPEATABLE READ` (Snapshot Isolation), Alice and Bob both check `SELECT count(*) FROM on_call WHERE active=true` (returns 2) and update their own separate rows to `active=false`, leaving 0 active doctors.
quizzes.question: Which concurrency anomaly occurred and how do you eliminate it reliably?
options: Dirty Read; switch to Read Uncommitted
Write Skew; upgrade to `SERIALIZABLE` (SSI + retry) or explicitly lock a shared parent/shift row via `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`
Cache Penetration; add a CDN
Split-brain; add Consistent Hashing
quizzes.explanation: Write Skew arises when concurrent Snapshot transactions read a shared set and modify disjoint rows. SSI (`SERIALIZABLE`) or materializing/locking a shared parent row closes the window.

quizzes.scenario: You switch a critical scheduling transaction to `ISOLATION LEVEL SERIALIZABLE` in PostgreSQL to guarantee zero Write Skew.
quizzes.question: What MUST your backend application code implement to remain reliable under concurrency?
options: Disable connection pooling
Bounded idempotent retry logic whenever the DB raises serialization failure `SQLSTATE 40001`
Turn off WAL logging
Cache SQL queries in DNS
quizzes.explanation: Optimistic SSI aborts conflicting transactions with `40001` instead of blocking readers; callers must safely retry the transaction.

quizzes.scenario: You are building an AI assistant UI that streams tokens from server to browser plus occasional user cancel requests over HTTP.
quizzes.question: Which realtime transport gives the simplest browser reliability, HTTP/2 multiplexing, and automatic cursor resume?
options: 1-second HTTP short polling
Raw UDP packets from browser JS
Server-Sent Events (SSE) over HTTPS with `Last-Event-ID` + standard `POST` for cancel
Opening a separate TCP port per token
quizzes.explanation: SSE excels for server-to-client streaming: it multiplexes over HTTP/2, traverses proxies cleanly, and natively sends `Last-Event-ID` on reconnect.

quizzes.scenario: A live sports chat has 500k concurrent WebSocket connections across 100 edge gateway pods, and 2% of mobile users on slow 3G fall 30 seconds behind.
quizzes.question: How should the WebSocket gateway protect healthy users from an OOM crash triggered by those slow consumers?
options: Block the entire room broadcast until all 500k TCP ACKs arrive
Enforce bounded per-connection outbound send buffers with drop-oldest or disconnect-and-resync policies
Buffer all unread frames indefinitely in gateway heap RAM
Switch all connections back to DNS TXT polling
quizzes.explanation: Applying per-socket backpressure high-water marks isolates slow consumers so one stalled socket cannot exhaust gateway memory and take down other connections.

quizzes.scenario: Your `likes_counter` table is hash-sharded by `post_id` across 32 DB shards, yet Shard #14 hits 100% CPU whenever a pop star posts.
quizzes.question: Which technique fixes the single-shard write hotspot cleanly?
options: Increase the hash modulus from 32 to 256 without changing keys
Switch partitioning key to `post_id` B-tree range partitioning
Salt the hot key (`post_id#0..15`) for partitioned writes + aggregate on reads/cache
Turn off replication on Shard #14
quizzes.explanation: Because all writes share one `post_id`, adding more shards alone still hashes that key to one shard. Bounded key salting spreads writes across 16 shards.

quizzes.scenario: Your team shards an audit log table by monotonically increasing `created_at` timestamp ranges (`DAY_2026_11_17`).
quizzes.question: What operational bottleneck immediately emerges at scale?
options: 100% of current writes hit the single newest day shard while older shards sit idle
Time-range queries can no longer use indexes
JSON serialization becomes twice as large
TLS certificates expire faster
quizzes.explanation: Monotonic range keys concentrate all live writes on the latest active partition; prepending a hash prefix or using hash partitioning eliminates the hot tail.

quizzes.scenario: Worker A acquires a Redis `SET lock_key token NX PX 10000` lease, hits a 14-second JVM GC pause right before writing to S3/DB, and then sends its write.
quizzes.question: What prevents Worker A's stale write from corrupting data already modified by Worker B (which acquired the lock at t=11s)?
options: Extending Redis TTL to 15 seconds
Have the lock service issue monotonically increasing fencing tokens that the storage layer rejects if `token <= last_seen_token`
Running `NTP` every 5 seconds on Worker A
Using `GETDEL` before Worker A exits
quizzes.explanation: Process pauses happen even with longer TTLs or clock sync. Only monotonic fencing tokens validated by the target storage server defeat delayed stale writes.

quizzes.scenario: You need a strongly consistent lock manager for cluster leader election rather than best-effort cache deduplication.
quizzes.question: Which mechanism provides linearizable leases and monotonic fencing tokens safe across single-node failovers?
options: A single un-replicated Memcached instance
Consensus-backed lease systems such as etcd or ZooKeeper using Raft/Zab + revision/zxid fencing tokens
Round-robin DNS records with 5-second TTL
Client-side `Math.random()` UUIDs
quizzes.explanation: Consensus stores commit leases via quorum and emit strictly increasing cluster revisions/zxids that remain valid across leader failover.

quizzes.scenario: An Order service executes `COMMIT` in PostgreSQL and then calls `kafka.send(orderCreated)`. During a brief network blip, the Kafka call times out after Postgres committed.
quizzes.question: What architectural fix eliminates dropped events or phantom events without slow 2PC?
options: Publish to Kafka before starting the PostgreSQL transaction
Write the event to an `outbox` table inside the same local ACID transaction and stream it via WAL-based CDC (Debezium)
Ignore Kafka errors and rely on daily manual checks
Set `acks=0` on the Kafka producer
quizzes.explanation: Publishing before COMMIT creates phantom events on rollback; publishing after COMMIT drops events on crashes. Transactional Outbox + CDC guarantees atomic state + event capture.

quizzes.scenario: Your Debezium CDC relay restarts after a pod eviction and re-reads the last unacknowledged Postgres WAL LSN offset.
quizzes.question: What delivery guarantee does Outbox + CDC provide downstream consumers, and what must consumers implement?
options: Strict no-retry delivery; consumers need nothing
At-least-once delivery; consumers must deduplicate using `event_id` in an idempotent sink/inbox table
Best-effort lossy delivery; consumers must poll Postgres
Synchronous RPC locking across all services
quizzes.explanation: If a relay crashes after producing to Kafka but before checkpointing its LSN offset, it replays those WAL events on restart—making consumer idempotency mandatory.

quizzes.scenario: In a Travel Booking Saga (`Flight -> Hotel -> Payment`), Flight and Hotel succeed, then Payment fails permanently due to insufficient funds.
quizzes.question: How does the Saga restore global consistency?
options: Hold open database `XA PREPARE` row locks across all three services until the user adds money
Execute backward compensating transactions (`CancelHotel`, then `CancelFlight`) with idempotent retries
Leave Flight and Hotel reserved until the next cron sweep
Drop the Payment service database indexes
quizzes.explanation: Because earlier local ACID steps already committed, a Saga runs semantic compensating actions in reverse order rather than rolling back a distributed lock.

quizzes.scenario: Because Sagas lack global Isolation (I in ACID), User B reads an intermediate order status `INVENTORY_RESERVED` before User A's Saga compensates and cancels it.
quizzes.question: What standard semantic countermeasure prevents dirty reads from exposing half-finished Saga state?
options: Use `PENDING` / `CONFIRMING` provisional states (Semantic Lock) that UI/queries handle explicitly until the Saga finalizes
Turn off foreign keys across all microservices
Convert all HTTP endpoints to `GET` requests
Disable connection pooling
quizzes.explanation: Marking records with explicit intermediate statuses (`PENDING_PAYMENT`) acts as a semantic lock so downstream flows distinguish unsettled Saga state from finalized state.

quizzes.scenario: A flaky mobile network causes a client to fire two identical `POST /v1/charges` requests 120ms apart with the same `Idempotency-Key: k-99`.
quizzes.question: How should the server respond to the second request arriving while the first is still running?
options: Process a second charge so the user sees fast feedback
Detect the `IN_PROGRESS` key lock and return `409 Conflict` (or wait briefly) rather than executing the charge twice
Delete the first database row and restart
Return `200 OK` with an empty JSON body
quizzes.explanation: Atomic key reservation (`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING`) detects an in-flight execution and prevents double charges while concurrent requests race.

quizzes.scenario: Downstream Fraud-Score service latency degrades from 20ms to 4000ms. Upstream Checkout threads all pile up waiting for 5s timeouts and crash Checkout.
quizzes.question: Which combination stops cascading thread-pool exhaustion immediately?
options: Increase Checkout HTTP timeout from 5s to 60s and add 10 synchronous retries
Per-dependency Bulkhead isolation + Circuit Breaker opening on error/slow-call threshold with fast fallback + jittered probe in Half-Open
Double Checkout JVM heap without changing timeouts
Disable health checks so Kubernetes keeps sending traffic
quizzes.explanation: Circuit Breakers trip open to fail fast without exhausting threads, Bulkheads cap blast radius, and Half-Open probes safely verify recovery.

quizzes.scenario: For a 20,000-seat stadium drop, 800,000 users refresh the seat map simultaneously at launch second.
quizzes.question: Which two components keep the Postgres `seats` table from melting under lock contention and repeated queries?
options: CDN-cached/pushed static seat-map snapshots + a FIFO/randomized Virtual Waiting Room admitting users in controlled batches
Using `SELECT * FROM seats FOR UPDATE` on page load for all 800,000 users
Putting every user's browser on direct SQL connections
Disabling HTTP caching headers on the venue layout
quizzes.explanation: Serving read-heavy seat availability from edge/Redis snapshots and throttling checkout entry via a Virtual Waiting Room caps OLTP concurrency to manageable capacity.

quizzes.scenario: Two friends select Seat A12 within 3 milliseconds of each other right as holds expire.
quizzes.question: What enforces the absolute final guarantee that Seat A12 can NEVER be sold twice even if Redis evicts early?
options: Client-side `localStorage` flag
A database unique constraint on `(event_id, seat_id)` paired with optimistic/atomic conditional update (`WHERE status = 'AVAILABLE'` or matching hold token)
A 100ms `sleep()` in Node/Python
CDN edge TTL invalidation
quizzes.explanation: Redis accelerates fast short-lived holds, while the relational DB's ACID unique constraint serves as the unbreakable source of truth against double booking.

quizzes.scenario: A merchant wallet balance sits in PostgreSQL under high concurrent payouts and refunds.
quizzes.question: Why should your core accounting database store immutable double-entry ledger lines (`debit_account`, `credit_account`, `amount`) alongside cached balances?
options: It lets you reconstruct every balance change cryptographically/auditably and guarantee zero money creation or destruction (`SUM == 0`)
It eliminates the need for indexes
It replaces TLS encryption on API calls
It reduces row count compared to single balance overwrites
quizzes.explanation: Double-entry accounting creates an immutable audit trail where every dollar moving out of one account matches a balanced credit in another.

quizzes.scenario: Your Payment Executor calls an external bank PSP, receives `504 Gateway Timeout`, and does not know whether the card was charged.
quizzes.question: What is the safest next action?
options: Tell the user payment succeeded immediately
Keep the ledger intent in `AMBIGUOUS / PENDING_RECON`, query PSP status / await webhook with the same idempotency key, and reconcile against T+1 settlement files
Reverse the local DB transaction and charge a different card
Retry forever in a tight `while True` loop
quizzes.explanation: Network timeouts are ambiguous—the remote bank may have committed. Holding an explicit pending state plus idempotent status polling + settlement reconciliation avoids double charges or lost funds.

quizzes.scenario: A creator uploads a 2-hour 4K raw `.mov` master. Transcoding sequentially on one beefy worker takes 4 hours.
quizzes.question: How do large streaming platforms cut encoding latency down to minutes?
options: Ask creators to upload 360p only
Split the master at GOP boundaries into 4–6s chunks and fan them across parallel stateless encoder workers outputting HLS/DASH ladders into object storage
Stream raw uncompressed frames directly from the upload server
Store the entire video inside Redis
quizzes.explanation: Chunk-level GOP splitting lets a DAG orchestrator encode every bitrate (360p..4K) and codec across dozens of workers in parallel, then stitch the `.m3u8`/`.mpd` manifest.

quizzes.scenario: Millions of viewers watch a top trending series concurrently during prime time, saturating regional ISP peering links.
quizzes.question: How do platforms avoid traversing the public transit internet for 90%+ of video bytes?
options: Pre-position hot catalog segments on dedicated ISP-embedded CDN appliances (e.g., Open Connect / Edge PoPs) steered by client control-plane steering
Switch video transport to synchronous WebSockets
Disable adaptive bitrate switching
Re-encode every stream on the fly per viewer
quizzes.explanation: Embedding NVMe edge appliances directly inside ISP networks serves immutable popular `.m4s` chunks one hop away from subscribers.

quizzes.scenario: Billing v2.1 rolls out alongside existing Tax v2.0 pods while adding `optional string tax_jurisdiction = 14` to a shared `.proto` message.
quizzes.question: Which action MUST you avoid so v2.0 and v2.1 pods coexist without breaking wire serialization?
options: Reusing deleted tag #5 for a brand-new unrelated enum field
Passing `UnknownFieldSet` through unchanged in relay proxies
Validating `FULL_TRANSITIVE` compatibility in CI
Using explicit optional fields with safe defaults
quizzes.explanation: Never reuse retired Protobuf tag numbers—historic persisted payloads and un-upgraded services still decode tag #5 with old semantics.

quizzes.scenario: An upstream webhook accidentally emits malformed binary bytes onto Kafka Partition 3 of `billing.events`.
quizzes.question: What keeps Partition 3 from stalling indefinitely behind crash-looping consumer restarts?
options: Set `retries=infinite` inside deserialization
Catch schema contract errors at the consumer boundary, emit raw frame + trace ID to `billing.dlq`, and commit offset cleanly
Turn off Avro/Protobuf parsing completely
Delete the Kafka topic partition
quizzes.explanation: Quarantining poison-pill schema errors into a monitored Dead-Letter Queue keeps valid invoices moving smoothly.

quizzes.scenario: Your API gateway fans out every user dashboard call across 25 parallel microservices, each holding `p99 = 45ms`.
quizzes.question: Roughly what fraction of user dashboard loads exceed 45ms, and what reduces that tail spike?
options: ~1% overall; increase thread pool size
~22.2% (`1 - 0.99^25`); enforce shard deadlines + bounded hedged requests after p95
0.04%; rely solely on average latency metrics
100%; switch internal RPCs from gRPC to XML
quizzes.explanation: Parallel fan-out amplifies individual 1% tail probabilities (`1 - 0.99^25 = 22.2%`); idempotent hedged requests cut p99 dramatically within a capped retry budget.

quizzes.scenario: Flash traffic triples gateway ingress from 500k to 1.5M RPS, filling downstream FIFO buffers past the CoDel sojourn threshold.
quizzes.question: What preserves `< 50ms` p99 SLA for healthy priority traffic?
options: Queue every request infinitely until downstream recovers
Shed low-priority excess requests fast (<0.5ms) using CoDel / Little's Law concurrency bounds with `429 Retry-After` jitter
Disable TLS session resumption
Force every gateway call to hit the auth database synchronously
quizzes.explanation: Failing fast above the Little's Law knee keeps admitted requests below SLA instead of timing out 100% of users.

quizzes.scenario: Your financial audit engine receives 150k immutable writes/s AND must answer 5-billion-row quarterly range aggregations under 2s.
quizzes.question: Which hybrid storage architecture eliminates both B-Tree random write amplification AND OLAP query interference?
options: Single unpartitioned PostgreSQL B-Tree running `GROUP BY` live
Hot LSM-Tree shards (WAL + MemTable + Bloom filters) compacting immutable slices into Dictionary/RLE-compressed Parquet on S3
Storing 5 years of ledger entries in browser localStorage
Disabling WAL crash recovery on PostgreSQL
quizzes.explanation: LSM handles high-throughput sequential ingest cleanly, while sorted compressed Parquet lets vectorized SIMD scanners prune 90%+ of irrelevant bytes.

quizzes.scenario: During 400k/s bursts, RocksDB flushes unmerged L0 SSTables faster than background threads compact L0->L1.
quizzes.question: What directly breaks both write latency AND read amplification unless mitigated?
options: L0 compaction write stalls & cross-SSTable read seeks; mitigate with reserved compaction NVMe IOPS + per-SSTable Bloom filters
DNS TTL expiry on ledger queries
UTF-8 byte encoding overhead
TCP Nagle buffering
quizzes.explanation: Unthrottled MemTable flushes exhaust L0 thresholds into write stalls; isolating compaction IOPS and sizing Bloom filters (~10 bits/key) keeps reads and writes fast.

quizzes.scenario: External merchants are pinned to `2024-05-01` JSON shapes while internal Billing & Tax teams ship canonical Protobuf structs weekly.
quizzes.question: How do Principal engineers honor TPP Orthogonality & Design by Contract here?
options: Embed 12 date-version `if/else` branches inside every Billing microservice
Translate merchant-pinned REST payloads into latest canonical Protobuf at Edge Contract Adapters
Force every external merchant to migrate synchronously each Friday
Drop JSON validation altogether
quizzes.explanation: Edge version adapters absorb external compatibility debt cleanly so internal microservices evolve rapidly on one canonical contract.

quizzes.scenario: A buggy merchant script submits a $999 charge using the EXACT same `Idempotency-Key` it previously used for a $10 charge.
quizzes.question: How must the idempotency ledger catch this bug safely?
options: Replay the old $10 receipt silently
Execute a second $999 charge immediately
Verify stored `payload_sha256` matches the incoming request body and return `422 Unprocessable Entity` on mismatch
Delete the earlier payment record
quizzes.explanation: Checking payload SHA-256 alongside `(merchant_id, key)` catches accidental client key reuse bugs immediately.

quizzes.scenario: Editors in Tokyo and London lose trans-Atlantic sync for 10 minutes, edit overlapping paragraphs offline, and later reconnect.
quizzes.question: Which replication strategy converges identically with ZERO dropped keystrokes and zero central lock server?
options: Wall-clock Last-Write-Wins (LWW) overwrite
Multi-leader edge hubs syncing associative, commutative, idempotent Sequence CRDT operations (`(clock, peerId)`)
Single-leader synchronous Postgres locks across the Pacific
HTTP short polling every 5 seconds
quizzes.explanation: Sequence CRDTs guarantee deterministic Strong Eventual Consistency across offline partitions without clock-skew overwrites.

quizzes.scenario: Document storage grows from 8 to 16 shard nodes while also serving Workspace Dashboard tag searches.
quizzes.question: Which partitioning + index strategy avoids cluster-wide key rehashing AND scatter-gather tail spikes?
options: `hash(doc_id) % N` + Local secondary indexes
Fixed virtual logical buckets mapped via etcd Consistent Hashing + async Global Term Index with `X-Min-Causal-Epoch` session tokens
Monotonic timestamp range sharding on document IDs
Broadcasting every key lookup to all 16 nodes
quizzes.explanation: Logical virtual buckets transfer whole shards cleanly on scale, while Global indexes + causal session tokens deliver O(1) reads with Read-Your-Own-Writes consistency.

quizzes.scenario: Subway riders lose connectivity after swiping cards, delivering transaction events to Kafka 90 seconds out of order.
quizzes.question: How does a 1M TPS Flink fraud pipeline still score 5-minute card velocity windows accurately?
options: Score strictly on ingestion wall-clock processing time
Drive sliding windows via Event-Time Watermarks paired with bounded `allowedLateness`
Run hourly `GROUP BY` cron jobs on the payment database
Drop any packet delayed >5 seconds
quizzes.explanation: Event-Time Watermarks + bounded `allowedLateness` compute accurate behavioral windows regardless of network jitter.

quizzes.scenario: You need to evaluate fraud velocity counters, ML classifiers, and user Activity Feed projections independently at 1M TPS.
quizzes.question: Which architectural combination avoids dual writes AND temporal coupling across teams?
options: Direct synchronous REST calls from Checkout to Fraud, Feed, and Elasticsearch
Transactional Outbox + Debezium WAL CDC -> Kafka log -> Keyed Flink Actors + Blackboard risk signals + idempotent CQRS sinks
Nightly SQL dumps via FTP
Two-Phase Commit (`XA PREPARE`) locking Checkout across Flink and Elasticsearch
quizzes.explanation: Outbox CDC eliminates dual-write divergence, while Actors + Blackboards + idempotent sinks scale orthogonally to 1M+ events/sec.
